A dictum is an authoritative statement — something said by a person (or institution) whose words carry weight, and therefore the statement is taken seriously or accepted as a guiding principle. Think of it as a "word from on high." The word is formal in register, which means you would rarely hear it in casual conversation; instead, you'd encounter it in legal writing, academic texts, journalism, and formal speech.

The noun has two closely related but slightly distinct senses, and understanding both will give you the full picture.

This is a declaration or ruling made by someone with authority — a judge, a philosopher, a senior expert, or an institution — that is meant to guide, settle, or define something. The key idea is that it comes from a position of power or expertise, and people are expected to follow it or at least take it very seriously.

Examples in sentences:

  • "The judge's dictum made it clear that such behaviour would not be tolerated in future cases."
  • "The committee issued a dictum that all reports must be submitted by Friday."
  • "The philosopher's famous dictum shaped how scientists approached the problem for centuries."

Notice that in each case, someone with authority is speaking, and the statement functions almost like a rule or a strong guiding word.

Sense 2: A well-known saying that expresses a general truth or principle

A dictum can also refer to a widely recognised maxim or saying — the kind of statement that has been around long enough, and repeated often enough, that it has taken on the feel of established wisdom. This sense overlaps with words like maxim, adage, or axiom.

Examples in sentences:

  • "The old dictum 'actions speak louder than words' still holds true today."
  • "She lived by the dictum that kindness costs nothing."
  • "The dictum 'innocent until proven guilty' is a cornerstone of modern law."

In this sense, the authority doesn't come from a specific living person, but from tradition, repetition, and the weight of experience behind the saying.

In law, "dictum" has a very specific and important use that you will almost certainly come across. Judges, when writing their decisions, sometimes make remarks or observations that go beyond what is strictly necessary to decide the case in front of them. These side comments are called obiter dicta (often shortened to just dicta, or a single one is called an obiter dictum). "Obiter" means "by the way" — so an obiter dictum is something the judge says "by the way," which is not the actual legal ruling.

This distinction matters enormously in law. The actual ruling (called the ratio decidendi) is binding — future courts must follow it. But an obiter dictum is not binding. It is merely persuasive — other courts can choose to be guided by it, but they don't have to follow it.

Example to make this concrete:

Imagine a judge is ruling on a case about whether someone stole a bicycle. The judge decides: "Yes, this person is guilty of theft." That ruling is the binding part. But then the judge adds: "In my view, similar logic would also apply to cases involving digital theft of data." That second comment — the one about digital theft — was not necessary to decide this case. It's an obiter dictum. It's the judge thinking aloud. Future courts might find it useful and follow it, but they are not legally obligated to.

Dictum has two accepted plurals:

  • Dicta — the Latin plural, more commonly used in formal and legal writing.
  • Dictums — the anglicised plural, perfectly correct and used in everyday formal writing.

Both are right. You might see "the judge's dicta" in a law journal and "several useful dictums" in a newspaper, and both are fine.
The subtle feeling of the word

What makes "dictum" different from just saying "statement" or "quote" is the sense of authority and finality it carries. A statement is neutral — anyone makes statements. A dictum carries the implication that the person speaking has the standing to declare something, and that their declaration has lasting significance. When you call something a dictum, you're signalling that it isn't just an opinion thrown into conversation — it is a considered, weighty pronouncement worth remembering and possibly following.
Quick summary of all you need to remember:

A dictum is a formal, authoritative statement — either a ruling or declaration made by someone in power, or a widely accepted saying that expresses a general truth. In law, it specifically refers to a judge's remark that goes beyond the necessary ruling and is therefore persuasive but not binding. The plural is either dicta or dictums. The word always carries a sense of weight, authority, and seriousness.
